segments.title: Sea Flight and the Fleet Air Arm's global war
segments.summary: Sea Flight uses one pilot's wartime recollections to show how Fleet Air Arm squadrons escorted convoys and fought from carriers around the world.
segments.body: Hugh Popham's Sea Flight is a personal account of training and wartime service as a Hurricane pilot in the Fleet Air Arm. The memoir moves from North Atlantic convoy routes and the West Indies to Ceylon and Madagascar, showing the reach of British carrier aviation during the Second World War. The quoted passages cover routine patrols, aircraft returning with bullet damage, a missing Albacore crew and a low-level attack under fire. Later chapters follow service in HMS Illustrious, Campania and Striker, so the story reaches beyond one ship or campaign. The book offers a close view of daily danger and the Fleet Air Arm's worldwide commitments.

evidence.note: The review describes a Fleet Air Arm memoir, its convoy-patrol setting, a combat episode, and its contents.

segments.title: Hurricanes, HMS Anthony and Royal Marines in Madagascar
segments.summary: A Sea Flight combat passage shows Hurricanes, HMS Anthony, HMS Diamond and Royal Marines overcoming a defended harbour during the Madagascar fighting.
segments.body: Sea Flight recounts an action in which an enemy sloop can still cover a harbour and impede troops ashore. Six Hurricanes from HMS Indomitable make a low-level strafing attack through smoke and return fire, even though the pilots doubt what rifle-calibre machine-gun bullets can do to the ship's plating. They leave the sloop burning, but the air attack forms only part of the action. HMS Anthony then enters the harbour under fire and lands fifty Royal Marines, who capture the naval depot, while HMS Diamond follows. Carrier aircraft, surface ships and landing troops each contribute a different part of the harbour action.

evidence.note: The quoted memoir passage describes the sloop, six Hurricanes attacking under fire, Anthony landing fifty Royal Marines, Diamond entering, and the harbour action ending.

segments.title: Ark Royal's career, design debate and wreck photographs
segments.summary: Mike Rossiter's history follows HMS Ark Royal from development to loss while leaving room to question parts of its design narrative.
segments.body: Mike Rossiter's Ark Royal traces the carrier's operations and voyages from beginning to end. Its photographs, layout and even-handed treatment of the Skua and Swordfish support the full career history. The review questions the book's standardized account of the ship's development and design, so that part of the narrative remains open to debate. Photographs from the search for Ark Royal, including submerged Swordfish and Fulmar wreckage, connect the written history to physical evidence at the wreck site.

evidence.note: The review assesses the Ark Royal history, its design treatment, and photographs connected with the wreck search.

segments.title: Swordfish, Taranto and carrier-landing culture
segments.summary: A Swordfish history of the Taranto raid brings carrier aviation's operational effect together with the humour and hazards of wartime deck landings.
segments.body: David Wragg's Swordfish history of the Taranto raid combines exceptional photographs with lively writing and quotations from both sides of the conflict. A dark Fleet Air Arm joke about whether a pilot can swim captures the fatalism surrounding a bad carrier landing at sea. The selected voices give the book as much to say about service culture as about the raid. Andrew Cunningham's barbed recollection of a lavish pre-war visit with Admiral Riccardi brings personality, professional judgment and retrospective wartime criticism into the story of the later attack on the Italian fleet.

evidence.note: The review discusses the Swordfish book, its Taranto subject, a Fleet Air Arm landing joke, and the Cunningham-Riccardi anecdote.

segments.title: Naval Wings: a Swordfish pilot's wider war
segments.summary: Naval Wings follows a Fleet Air Arm Swordfish pilot from Mediterranean strikes to the Atlantic and the war against Japan.
segments.body: John Wellham's Naval Wings begins with his service in 824 Squadron aboard HMS Eagle. Wellham flew in the Swordfish attack on Bomba in which three torpedoes sank four ships, an episode presented as evidence of air power's growing place in naval warfare. He was then selected for the second strike on Taranto from HMS Illustrious. The memoir continues through Atlantic and anti-submarine operations to the final campaign against Japan with the British Pacific Fleet. Together, these episodes follow the Swordfish beyond its most famous raid and carry one Fleet Air Arm career across several theatres.

evidence.note: The review outlines Wellham's Swordfish service, the memoir's theatres, and its account of personal memory checked against records.

segments.title: How Naval Wings checks memory against official records
segments.summary: John Wellham explains how taped recollections, flying logbooks, photographs and official records were combined to create Naval Wings without hiding their disagreements.
segments.body: John Wellham explains that Naval Wings grew from taped recollections encouraged by the Fleet Air Arm Museum's curator and by questions from Wellham's family. He presents it as a personal record in his own words rather than a replacement for existing operational histories. His flying logbook and contemporary photographs support those memories, while official records provide checks on dates and squadron numbers. Those records sometimes disagree, and the museum helped investigate the disputed points. Wellham's method preserves the memoir's first-person value while allowing its claims to be checked against documentation.

evidence.note: Wellham's preface explains the taped-memory origins, use of logbooks and photographs, official-record checks, disagreements, and Fleet Air Arm Museum assistance.

segments.title: Flying through Red Sea mirage conditions
segments.summary: A Naval Wings passage shows how black-painted petrol drums marked a desert runway when continuous mirage obscured the pilots' sense of height.
segments.body: Wellham describes reaching a Red Sea airfield after an eight-hour flight. Near-continuous mirage made height over the sand difficult to judge, turning the landing into a problem that had to be solved on the ground. Black-painted petrol drums marked virtual runway edges and served much like flare-path lights at night. The arrangement shows how air operations depended on local knowledge and improvised ground support as well as aircraft performance. The passage ends with dinner, beds and a bar for the aircrew, followed by an encounter with disgruntled army officers who thought they had been forgotten.

evidence.note: The quoted Red Sea passage describes an eight-hour flight, mirage-obscured height judgment, black-painted petrol drums marking runways, and the remote airfield's accommodations.
